extracted.intended_audience: scholars, graduate students, and researchers of public policy, administrative law, social movements, and notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how environmental justice (EJ) movement mobilization (public comments, coalitions, and attention) affects draft and final agency rules—measuring change in whether/how EJ is addressed across agencies and administrations. Includes hypotheses, operational measures (comments, unique vs mass comments, agency receptivity), and proposed mechanisms (distributive information, constituency signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive Claims Hypothesis (Hypothesis 4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers are more likely to change whether or how policies address distributive justice when commenters raise distributive justice concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: commenters draw attention to distributional impacts (who a policy may affect). Agencies have incentives (e.g., EO 12898, APA/NEPA review) to address distributive concerns. Competing intuition: distributive claims may not provide new technical information and thus may be ignored; policymakers may already anticipate EJ concerns and state final positions in drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated Claims Hypothesis (Hypothesis 4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers are more likely to change whether or how policies address concerns when more commenters raise them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes unique comments (approximate coalition size—different groups submitting unique text) from mass comments (signatures/form letters indicating public attention). Theory: repeated information and coalition size increase influence. Competing intuition: repetition without technical novelty may be discounted; large salience may lead agencies to preempt critiques in drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Receptivity Hypothesis (Hypothesis 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers who more frequently address concerns like environmental justice will be more responsive to commenters raising those concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies differ in norms, missions, and epistemic communities; those with histories of addressing EJ (or whose mission aligns with EJ) should be more receptive. Competing intuition: agencies familiar with EJ may anticipate and already incorporate responses in drafts, making them less responsive to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Attention Hypothesis (Hypothesis 4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed policies are more likely to change when they receive more public attention (e.g., more public comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: higher public attention signals salience and may prompt policy revision. Competing intuition: high comment volume might indicate processes already salient to agencies, which would have pre-stated final positions in drafts; alternately, public attention may be unrelated to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Pressure Hypothesis (Hypothesis 4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies are more likely to address an issue when they receive more public attention (e.g., more public comments) and at least one comment raises that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an interactional claim: the total number of comments conditions whether an issue-raised-by-at-least-one-comment leads to substantive/addressing changes. Competing intuition: anticipated scrutiny in high-attention rulemakings may reduce change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: response to environmental justice claims in policy documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary dependent variable is discursive: whether and how draft and final rules address environmental justice concerns (e.g., adding EJ language where draft did not, or changing sections that already address EJ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats textual changes about EJ as 'lobbying success' for EJ activists; this is distinct from (but complementary to) substantive policy changes. Methods include tracing evolution of EJ analyses across drafts and finals and measuring whether commenters' EJ claims are reflected in final text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure: number of comments mobilized (overall and EJ-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of comments received on a draft rule (both total comments and comments specifically raising EJ concerns) as predictors of whether EJ is later addressed in policy texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: more groups and individuals raising EJ concerns correlate with policy text changes. Guidance notes to control for overall public attention and distinguish EJ-specific counts from general comment volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure: unique comments versus mass (identical/form) comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique comments approximate coalition size (different organizations submitting different texts); mass comments (signatures on identical form letters) indicate public attention/pressure but not coalition diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should distinguish unique from mass comments because they capture different dimensions (coalition breadth vs amplitude of public pressure). Note: most individual comments are mobilized by interest groups; unaffiliated individual comments are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency receptivity / mission-alignment as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of EJ comments on policy change varies by agency; agencies with missions focused on environmental and distributive policy are more likely to respond to EJ claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect sizes vary across agencies—interpretation: agencies' institutional identities, missions, and norms prime them to be receptive. Empirical strategy: test heterogeneity across agencies and classify agencies by mission or historical responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism: political information about a policy's disparate effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about who will be affected by a policy (distributive impacts) are a form of political information that can change policymakers' perceptions and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such information need not be technical—any actor can highlight communities of concern. These claims assert deservingness and may require revisions. Courts and EO 12898 increase agencies' incentives to consider distributional impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism: mobilization demonstrates constituency (constitutency signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions and letter-writing campaigns provide evidence that a group represents an engaged, issue-specific constituency; this signal is politically valuable given many groups are 'memberless' or professionalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: showing an actual constituency differentiates claimants from professional lobbyists and may strengthen political claims. Form letters and petition signatures are among the few ways to demonstrate constituency in rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers may anticipate certain critiques (e.g., EJ concerns) and thus state their final positions in draft rules, which reduces the observed impact of subsequent comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This competing mechanism is repeated throughout hypotheses: large comment counts or well-known issues may yield less observable change because agencies preemptively address them. Empirical analyses should account for potential preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and case-selection bias critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that select high-salience or landmark cases may overstate (or understate) advocacy effects; systematic, large-scale analysis across many rules is needed to avoid selecting on the dependent variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author motivates the dataset (all rules for 40 agencies, 1993–2020) to avoid bias in case selection. Guidance: use broad sampling across agencies and time to assess generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical information versus political/distributive information tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking privileges scientific and legal facts; technical/legal information is traditionally the 'currency' of influence, while activists typically supply political/distributive claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: claims lacking novel technical info may struggle to persuade agencies. Yet distributive claims may still matter via normative/political channels or when paired with public pressure or agency receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual metric: changes in policy sections that address EJ
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific operationalization: measure whether sections of a policy text that address EJ change between draft and final when EJ concerns are raised in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fine-grained measure of discursive change—use textual comparison methods and control for overall public attention to isolate EJ-specific effects. Examples: adding EJ language where absent, altering analyses of disparate impacts, or modifying mitigation/consideration language.
